LeaseKey names one shard of one stream; a store of your own keys its rows by the key's stream:shard form. Every LeaseStore call names its shard by a LeaseKey. The stream is the name the subscription's KinesisStream was given, and the shard is the id the service assigned. Shard ids repeat across streams, so a store keys by both, and one store serves every stream of a broker. LeaseKey displays as stream:shard; a stream name holds no colon, so the form is unambiguous, and a store that keeps one string key writes it. A store of your own implements the five methods of LeaseStore and is installed with KinesisBroker::lease_store. A store for one instance grants every lease; a store for several instances makes acquire, renew and checkpoint conditional on the owner, as DynamoLeaseStore does.

A store for one instance keeps its checkpoints in a map keyed by the key's string form. examples/kinesis_leases_key.rs /// Each shard's progress in a string-keyed map, for a single instance that owns every shard. #[derive(Debug, Default)] struct Checkpoints(Mutex<HashMap<String, LeaseState>>); impl LeaseStore for Checkpoints { fn checkpoint<'a>( &'a self, key: &'a LeaseKey, _owner: &'a str, sequence: &'a str, ) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<bool, LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async move { self.0 .lock() .map_err(|err| err.to_string())? .entry(key.to_string()) .or_default() .checkpoint = Some(sequence.to_owned()); Ok(true) }) } fn record_opened_at<'a>( &'a self, key: &'a LeaseKey, _owner: &'a str, sequence: &'a str, ) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<bool, LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async move { self.0 .lock() .map_err(|err| err.to_string())? .entry(key.to_string()) .or_default() .opened_at = Some(sequence.to_owned()); Ok(true) }) } fn read<'a>(&'a self, key: &'a LeaseKey) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<LeaseState, LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async move { let state = self .0 .lock() .map_err(|err| err.to_string())? .get(&key.to_string()) .cloned(); Ok(state.unwrap_or_default()) }) } // One instance owns every shard, so a lease is always granted and never lapses. fn acquire<'a>( &'a self, _key: &'a LeaseKey, _owner: &'a str, _ttl: Duration, ) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<bool, LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async { Ok(true) }) } fn renew<'a>( &'a self, _key: &'a LeaseKey, _owner: &'a str, _ttl: Duration, ) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<bool, LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async { Ok(true) }) } fn release<'a>( &'a self, _key: &'a LeaseKey, _owner: &'a str, ) -> BoxFuture<'a, Result<(), LeaseError>> { Box::pin(async { Ok(()) }) } } The service installs it on its broker. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_leases_key.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker, checkpoints: Arc<Checkpoints>) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("loyalty", "0.1.0")).with_broker( broker.lease_store(checkpoints), |b| { b.include(credit); }, ) } examples/manual/kinesis_leases_key.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker, checkpoints: Arc<Checkpoints>) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("loyalty", "0.1.0")).with_broker( broker.lease_store(checkpoints), |b| { b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("loyalty"), Credit).build()); }, ) }

legacy_stream names the stream a table's bare shard rows belong to, so a table written by an earlier version resumes from them. Earlier versions of this crate keyed a row by the shard id alone, such as shardId-000000000000. A bare row names no stream, and every stream's first shard has that id. So DynamoLeaseStore reads a bare row only for the stream legacy_stream names. A shard of that stream with no checkpoint under its own stream:shard row resumes from its bare row, and the first read copies the checkpoint to the new row. A checkpoint already on the new row wins over the bare one. Other streams ignore the bare rows. Without legacy_stream, a shard whose bare row holds a checkpoint is refused with a lease error that names the table, the shard and the stream, and it is not read until the stream is named or the row is deleted. Once the upgraded service has opened a subscription on every stream it reads, every bare row with progress has its copy; the rows whose lease_key holds no : can then be deleted, and the setting dropped. A table that served several streams before the upgrade holds, in each bare row, the checkpoint of whichever stream wrote last. No stream can resume from such a row: delete the bare rows and open each stream with start_at at the position it should read from. The two versions lease different rows, so an old and a new instance can read one shard at once; stop the old instances before the new ones start.

The table returns-leases served the stream returns alone before the upgrade. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_leases_legacy.rs /// The table was written by an earlier version for the stream `returns` alone, so its bare rows /// are that stream's progress. fn broker(config: &SdkConfig, table: &str) -> KinesisBroker { let leases = Arc::new(DynamoLeaseStore::new(config, table).legacy_stream("returns")); KinesisBroker::from_config(config.clone()).lease_store(leases) } examples/manual/kinesis_leases_legacy.rs /// The table was written by an earlier version for the stream `returns` alone, so its bare rows /// are that stream's progress. fn broker(config: &SdkConfig, table: &str) -> KinesisBroker { let leases = Arc::new(DynamoLeaseStore::new(config, table).legacy_stream("returns")); KinesisBroker::from_config(config.clone()).lease_store(leases) }

MemoryLeaseStore is the default store: correct for one service instance, and empty again after a restart. A broker that names no lease store creates one with MemoryLeaseStore::new. It keeps leases and checkpoints in the memory of the process, so one instance reads every shard of its streams and orders a split's children after their parents. Brokers of one process that share it through an Arc share its leases and checkpoints. A new process starts with an empty store. So a restarted service opens each shard at the tip, unless start_at names another position. The records published while the service was down are not read, and a held record does not come back. A service that must resume where it stopped, or runs in more than one instance, uses a store outside the process, such as DynamoLeaseStore.

owner_id names this instance in the lease table; left out, each broker takes an id of its own, unique to that broker. A lease store records which owner holds each shard, and grants an owner the leases it already holds. So an instance that restarts under the same id takes its shards back at once, without waiting for its old leases to expire. A stable name per instance, such as a pod name, gives that. A fixed id must never be shared by two instances that run at the same time: both would hold the same shards, and each would read them. The DynamoLeaseStore table shows the id in the lease_owner column of each row, which tells an operator which instance reads which shard.

The dispatch service names each instance after its host. KinesisPosition names a place in the stream: the trim horizon, the tip, an arrival timestamp on every shard, or one record of one shard. A stream keeps its records for its retention period, so a subscription can be moved through them, at startup with start_at or from a handler with a seek. By default each shard resumes from its checkpoint, and a shard without one opens at the tip. Position Scope Meaning KinesisPosition::horizon() every shard the trim horizon: the oldest record the stream still retains KinesisPosition::latest() every shard the tip: only records published from now on KinesisPosition::timestamp(millis) every shard on each shard, the first record that arrived at or after that instant, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch KinesisPosition::sequence(shard, sequence) one shard exactly one record, by its shard id and sequence number The first three apply to every shard the subscription reads. A timestamp is matched against the arrival time the service stamped on each record, which the service calls approximate: records that arrived within the same moment are not told apart. A sequence position names one shard and moves no other. A delivery's own place is a sequence position: Ctx<Position> binds it, and a seek there reads that record again. The type is also what the core's Positioned returns for a delivered record.

A report is rebuilt from the readings that arrived since an instant its configuration names. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_positions_timestamp.rs /// Adds a reading to the report. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("readings"))] async fn report(reading: &Reading) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(reading.sensor, reading.value, "reading reported"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The report opens every shard at the first reading that arrived at or after `since`, in /// milliseconds since the Unix epoch. fn service(broker: KinesisBroker, since: u64) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(report.start_at(KinesisPosition::timestamp(since))); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_positions_timestamp.rs /// Adds a reading to the report. struct Report; impl Handle<Reading> for Report { fn handle( &self, reading: &Reading, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(reading.sensor, reading.value, "reading reported"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The report opens every shard at the first reading that arrived at or after `since`, in /// milliseconds since the Unix epoch. fn service(broker: KinesisBroker, since: u64) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(KinesisStream::new("readings"), Report) .build() .start_at(KinesisPosition::timestamp(since)), ); }) }

A handler moves its running subscription through the SeekHandle key; a sequence position moves one shard, the others move every shard. Ctx<SeekHandle> binds a KinesisSeeker for the subscription the delivery came from. Its seek(position) takes a KinesisPosition and returns once the shards it moves read from there. The horizon, the tip and a timestamp move every shard this instance reads. A sequence position moves only the shard it names, and that shard needs a live reader in this instance: a shard another instance reads, or one already finished, is refused with KinesisError::Read. Ctx<Position> gives the delivery's own sequence position to aim with. A seek moves this instance and no other. It writes no checkpoint: it starts the checkpoint bookkeeping of the shards it moves afresh, so an acknowledgement of a record delivered before the seek no longer moves the checkpoint. The next acknowledgement after the seek checkpoints from the new position. Records from that position onward are delivered again, which at-least-once delivery allows. A seek after the service shut down returns KinesisError::NotConnected. A batch handler reaches the same key through its KinesisBatchContext. A position that has to apply on every startup belongs in start_at instead.

The handler replays the retained backlog, and the marker job moves the subscription to the tip, so the rest of the backlog is skipped. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_seek.rs /// Replays the retained backlog; on the marker job it abandons the rest of it and follows the /// tip instead. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("jobs"), start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()))] async fn replay(job: &Job, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>) -> HandlerOutcome { if job.id == MARKER && seeker.seek(KinesisPosition::latest()).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(job.id, "job replayed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kinesis_seek.rs /// Replays the retained backlog; on the marker job it abandons the rest of it and follows the /// tip instead. struct Replay; impl Handle<Job, (), (), KinesisContext> for Replay { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if job.id == MARKER { ctx.context(SeekHandle) .seek(KinesisPosition::latest()) .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; } tracing::info!(job.id, "job replayed"); Ok(()) } }

start_at opens the subscription at a position you name on every startup, ahead of the stored checkpoints. It is a clause of the attribute, start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()), or .start_at(position) among the mount-site settings. The position lands on the shards the subscription opens with, ahead of their first read, whatever their checkpoints say. A reader that starts later in the run, after a failure or a takeover, resumes from its shard's checkpoint, or, without one, at the first record the shard's last reading read. A child shard of a split or a merge with no checkpoint of its own opens at its oldest record, so no record of a resharded key is skipped. A sequence position on a shard this instance does not read is refused, and the service stops at startup. It suits a read model rebuilt from the retained stream on each boot.

The audit projection is rebuilt from the oldest retained entry on every startup, although it checkpointed every entry it read before. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_positions_start_at.rs /// Rebuilds the audit projection from the oldest retained entry on every startup. #[subscriber( KinesisStream::new("ledger.audit"), start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()) )] async fn project(entry: &AuditEntry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "entry projected"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kinesis_positions_start_at.rs /// Projects every audit entry it reads. struct Project; impl Handle<AuditEntry> for Project { fn handle( &self, entry: &AuditEntry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "entry projected"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The projection is rebuilt from the oldest retained entry on every startup. b.include( subscriber(KinesisStream::new("ledger.audit"), Project) .build() .start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()), ); }) }

KinesisPublish, Publish in the prelude, writes each record with one PutRecord; it is the broker's default, so a reply needs no policy. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot, .out_retry(Publish::default()) for retry copies. after_startup(Publish::default(), ..) hands the same publisher to a startup hook. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into a KinesisPublisher. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through this one. A record goes to the stream its destination names: the reply type's #[outgoing(name)], a reply("stream") clause, or to("stream") on the publish. A stream is named by its name. A publish returns once the service has stored the record, or with the KinesisError::Publish it reported. The record hands the service the bytes the codec wrote, with the message's headers in an envelope in front of them when it has any. A stream takes a record of up to 1 MiB, data and partition key together, unless its owner raised the limit, which goes up to 10 MiB. Each record carries a partition key, which picks its shard and its order. A call names it with the partition_key step, and a mount site with KinesisPublishSettings.

The handler replies with a confirmation through the default policy and hands a shipment to a slot that names the policy. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_publishing_publish.rs /// Confirms each order with its return value and hands it to the warehouse through a slot. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher, Shipments>) -> Confirmation { let shipment = Shipment { order: order.id }; if let Err(err) = shipments.message(&shipment).publish().await { tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not published"); } Confirmation { order: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(KinesisBroker::new(), |b| { // The reply names no policy and takes the broker's default; the slot names one. b.include(confirm) .out(Shipments, Publish::default()) .build(); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_publishing_publish.rs /// Confirms each order with its return value and hands it to the warehouse through a slot. struct Confirm; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, Confirmation, Outs<(Entry,)>> for Confirm where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome> { let shipment = Shipment { order: order.id }; if let Err(err) = outs.get(Shipments).message(&shipment).publish().await { tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not published"); } Ok(Confirmation { order: order.id }) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(KinesisBroker::new(), |b| { // The reply names no policy and takes the broker's default; the slot names one. b.include( subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"), Confirm) .reply() .build(), ) .out(Shipments, Publish::default()) .build(); }) }

A record's partition key picks its shard and its order; four places can name it, and a record nobody keyed gets a process-unique one. The service hashes the key to pick the shard, so every record of one key lands on one shard, and a reader sees them in the order they were written. A key is 1 to 256 characters; the service refuses a record with any other with KinesisError::Publish. One key is one shard's write throughput, which the service limits per shard, so a key that every record shares orders them all at the cost of that throughput. The publisher takes the first key it finds, in this order: the partition_key step of the publish; the partition-key header, PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, that the message carries; the key the mount site named on the policy, with KinesisPublishSettings; a key unique to the process, which spreads the records over the shards. The header is the portable spelling: a body that names the key that way stays free of this crate, and a message that crossed from another broker of the framework carries its key in it. A message type declares the header in its typed header contract, #[outgoing(headers = ..)], with a field renamed to partition-key; a HeaderMap with that entry works the same. The key travels in the record's own partition-key field, and the header is left out of the envelope. On delivery the subscription reports the key under the same header.

Every shipment of one customer carries the customer as its key, so the warehouse reads them in order. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_publishing_keys.rs /// The header a shipment carries: `partition-key`, which becomes the record's partition key. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize)] struct ShipmentKey { #[serde(rename = "partition-key")] customer: String, } /// Every shipment of one customer lands on one shard, so its consumer sees them in order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments", headers = ShipmentKey)] struct Shipment { order: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; /// The body names no broker: the plain bound moves between brokers untouched. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher, Shipments>) -> HandlerOutcome { let key = ShipmentKey { customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let shipment = Shipment { order: order.id }; if shipments .message(&shipment) .with_headers(&key) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kinesis_publishing_keys.rs /// The header a shipment carries: `partition-key`, which becomes the record's partition key. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize)] struct ShipmentKey { #[serde(rename = "partition-key")] customer: String, } /// Every shipment of one customer lands on one shard, so its consumer sees them in order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments", headers = ShipmentKey)] struct Shipment { order: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; /// The body names no broker: the plain bound moves between brokers untouched. struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let key = ShipmentKey { customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let shipment = Shipment { order: order.id }; outs.get(Shipments) .message(&shipment) .with_headers(&key) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

The partition_key step keys one record on the publish builder; a body that names it bounds its slot on KinesisPublishOptions. The step stands among the framework's own: .message(..), .to(..), .partition_key(..), .publish(). It sets the key of this record only, and it wins over every other place a key can come from. The step comes from KinesisPublishSteps in the prelude. It is reachable where the publisher's options are Kinesis's, so the body bounds its slot as Out<impl Publisher<Options = KinesisPublishOptions>, Slot>. That bound is the one place a handler body says which broker it runs on. The step sets an option of the publish, and it wraps nothing. So the record still leaves through the entry the mount site named: that entry's codec encodes it, its transforms run, and a test attributes the publish to its slot. A test reads the options of a slot's publishes with tb.out::<Slot>().with_options(..).

Every journal entry of one tenant carries the tenant as its key, so the journal keeps each tenant's order. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_publishing_step.rs /// The slot the journal entries leave through. #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Journalled)] struct Journal; /// Every entry of one tenant lands on one shard, so the journal keeps each tenant's order. The /// bound on the options type puts the step within reach, and says that this body runs on /// Kinesis. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"))] async fn record( order: &Order, Out(journal): Out<impl Publisher<Options = KinesisPublishOptions>, Journal>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let sent = journal .message(&Journalled { order: order.id }) .partition_key(order.tenant.as_str()) .publish() .await; if sent.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kinesis_publishing_step.rs /// The slot the journal entries leave through. #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Journalled)] struct Journal; /// Every entry of one tenant lands on one shard, so the journal keeps each tenant's order. The /// bound on the options type puts the step within reach, and says that this body runs on /// Kinesis. struct Record; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Record where Entry: OutEntry<Journal, Wire: Publisher<Options = KinesisPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { outs.get(Journal) .message(&Journalled { order: order.id }) .partition_key(order.tenant.as_str()) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

partition_key at the mount site keys every record of a position, a reply included, which has no publish call to put a step on. A replying handler returns a value, and the runtime publishes it. So a reply has no publish builder for the partition_key step. KinesisPublishSettings::partition_key names the key on the policy instead, right after the position it applies to: .out_reply(Publish::default()).partition_key("receipts-v1"), or after .out(Slot, ..). KinesisPublish::partition_key is the same setting written on the policy value. The setting is available after this crate's policy and after no other broker's. The key ranks third among the places a key comes from, so a step or a partition-key header on a record wins over it. A retry copy carries the delivery's headers, its partition-key among them, so on the retry position the copy keeps the record's own key. A reply that needs a key of its own per delivery takes a publish transform at the mount site that writes partition_key into the options. The AsyncAPI document reports the key on the message object.

Every receipt carries one key, so all receipts land on one shard, in order. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_replies.rs use ruststream_kinesis::prelude::*; /// A receipt always goes to the receipts stream, so the type is where that stream is named. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } /// The handler names what it replies with; how that reply is published is the mount's. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(KinesisBroker::new(), |b| { // One key means one shard: every receipt is ordered against every other, at the cost of // a single shard's throughput. Leave it off to spread them instead. b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .partition_key("receipts-v1"); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_replies.rs use ruststream_kinesis::prelude::*; /// A receipt always goes to the receipts stream, so the type is where that stream is named. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } /// The body names what it replies with; how that reply is published is the mount's. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(KinesisBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"), Confirm) .reply() .build(), ) // One key means one shard: every receipt is ordered against every other, at the cost of // a single shard's throughput. Leave it off to spread them instead. .out_reply(Publish::default()) .partition_key("receipts-v1"); }) }

An ack is a per-shard checkpoint: it moves only when every earlier record is handled; drop retires a record, and a requeue is unsupported. A shard is an ordered log, and the service keeps no per-record state for a reader. So the subscription remembers one position per shard, the checkpoint, in the lease store. HandlerOutcome::ack marks the record handled. The checkpoint moves past it once every earlier record of the shard is handled too, and the lease store records the new position. HandlerOutcome::drop marks the record handled the same way, which is how a record the handler can never process is retired. HandlerOutcome::retry asks for a requeue, which a shard cannot perform; the runtime logs the refusal as a warning. The record stays unhandled, and the checkpoint stops in front of it while later records are still delivered and handled. It is read again, with every record after it, when the shard's lease is next taken: after a restart or when another instance takes the shard over. That needs a store that keeps checkpoints across a restart, such as DynamoLeaseStore; the default MemoryLeaseStore forgets them, and a restarted service opens each shard at the tip. Within one run the record does not come back. A registration that declares max_attempts turns retry into a counted copy published back to the stream, as retry_after does after a delay. Delivery is at-least-once: a record handled after the held one is delivered again when the shard is read from the checkpoint. A seek starts the checkpoint bookkeeping of the shards it moves afresh. In a TestApp test the in-process transport consults no lease store, and a held record does not come back there either.

An entry is booked, an empty one is retired, and a refund holds the checkpoint until the payment it returns is booked. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_settlement_outcomes.rs /// Books each entry. An empty entry is retired; a refund waits for the payment it returns, and /// holds the shard's checkpoint in front of it until then. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("ledger"))] async fn book(entry: &Entry) -> HandlerOutcome { match entry.amount { 0 => HandlerOutcome::drop(), amount if amount < 0 => HandlerOutcome::retry(), amount => { tracing::info!(entry.id, amount, "booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(book); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_settlement_outcomes.rs /// Books each entry. An empty entry is retired; a refund waits for the payment it returns, and /// holds the shard's checkpoint in front of it until then. struct Book; impl Handle<Entry> for Book { fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(match entry.amount { 0 => Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()), amount if amount < 0 => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), amount => { tracing::info!(entry.id, amount, "booked"); Ok(()) } }) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("ledger"), Book).build()); }) }

max_attempts(n) caps deliveries per record; dead_letter(stream) names the stream a spent record leaves for, and a cap without one retires the record. The cap counts the first delivery too. Kinesis keeps no delivery count, so the count travels with the record in RETRY_COUNT_HEADER. Under a cap every retry is a copy published back to the stream, the immediate retry too, because only a copy carries the count forward. When a retry would make the delivery the n-th one, the runtime settles it and publishes the record to the dead-letter stream instead, without the delay. The record keeps its payload, its headers and its partition key; its retry count says how many times it was delivered. A cap without a dead-letter stream checkpoints past the spent record, as drop does. The dead-letter stream is an ordinary stream of the service's own infrastructure: a subscription of the same service, or of another one, reads it.

An order gets four deliveries; the fourth one that still cannot be settled goes to orders.unsettled. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_retry.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Four deliveries per order, then the record leaves for a stream an operator reads. b.include(reconcile) .max_attempts(nonzero!(4)) .dead_letter("orders.unsettled"); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_retry.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Four deliveries per order, then the record leaves for a stream an operator reads. b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"), Reconcile).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(4)) .dead_letter("orders.unsettled"); }) }

out_retry(policy) replaces the publisher the retry copies leave through, so the copies take a transform or a codec of the mount site's choosing. A Kinesis registration publishes its retry copies without it, through the broker's default KinesisPublish policy. out_retry names the policy for that position, and the chain after it takes the position's steps: .transform(..) and .codec(..). A transform on the retry position reads the delivery it answers, through a PublishContext, and runs on every copy. The copy carries the record's own bytes, so a codec named there encodes nothing. The copy keeps the record's partition key and lands on that key's shard.

Every invoice copy says which stream it was deferred from. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_settlement_out_retry.rs /// Writes the stream a record was deferred from onto its retry copy. struct DeferredFrom; impl<Context, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<Context>, Options> for DeferredFrom { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, Context>, ) { out.headers_mut() .insert(DEFERRED_FROM, cx.name().to_owned()); } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(collect) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(DeferredFrom); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_settlement_out_retry.rs /// Writes the stream a record was deferred from onto its retry copy. struct DeferredFrom; impl<Context, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<Context>, Options> for DeferredFrom { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, Context>, ) { out.headers_mut() .insert(DEFERRED_FROM, cx.name().to_owned()); } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("invoices"), Collect).build()) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(DeferredFrom); }) }

retry_after(delay) publishes a copy of the record back to its stream once the delay is over, with the attempt count in a header; the copy arrives at the tip. Kinesis holds no record back and counts no deliveries, so the runtime does both. It settles the delivery, waits out the delay and publishes a copy of the record, payload and headers, to the stream the subscription reads. The descriptor reports that stream as the address of its copies, so the registration needs no publisher of its own. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER incremented, and the handler reads it like any other header. The copy keeps the record's partition key, so it lands on the shard of that key. It is a new record at the tip of that shard, so it loses its place among the records it was published with. Every consumer of the stream reads the copy, since it is an ordinary record of the stream. The copy waits in the service's memory, so it is at-most-once over the delay: a process that exits before the timer fires loses it. max_attempts(n) caps the deliveries of one record, and out_retry replaces the publisher the copies leave through. Where the order of a key matters more than the delay, a plain retry holds the shard's checkpoint instead.

An order that cannot be settled yet comes back thirty seconds later. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_retry.rs /// Asks for a pause when the order cannot be settled yet. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"))] async fn reconcile(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if settled(order.id) { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(PAUSE) } } fn settled(id: u64) -> bool { id.is_multiple_of(2) } examples/manual/kinesis_retry.rs /// Asks for a pause when the order cannot be settled yet. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<Order> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ready(if settled(order.id) { Ok(()) } else { Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(PAUSE)) }) } } fn settled(id: u64) -> bool { id.is_multiple_of(2) }

A stream name in #[subscriber] reads every shard of that stream; KinesisStream carries every other setting of the subscription. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the stream orders with the descriptor's defaults: KinesisStream::new("orders"). A stream is named by its name, which the service limits to 128 characters of letters, digits, _, . and -. The subscription finds the stream's shards, takes a lease on each one and reads each leased shard with its own reader. A shard resumes from its stored checkpoint, and a shard without one opens at the tip; start_at names another position. The subscription is open once every shard it took has a reader and a starting cursor, so a record published after startup reaches it. A stream the service does not have stops the service at startup, unless the descriptor creates it. Delivery is at-least-once, and an acknowledgement moves the shard's checkpoint, as Checkpoint describes. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, body).

The stream orders, read by one handler. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads every shard of the stream `orders`. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(place); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads every shard of the stream `orders`. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }) }

A slice handler gets up to batch(n) records; n becomes the GetRecords limit, and a short batch goes out 50 ms after its first record. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. Every shard reader asks GetRecords for at most n records, so one read never fetches more than one batch holds; the service caps a read at 10,000 records. A batch that is still filling goes to the handler 50 ms after its first record, so on a quiet stream a batch is often smaller than n. One batch mixes the records of every shard this instance reads. One outcome settles every record of the batch. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles record i with outcome i, and each record moves the checkpoint of its own shard. A retry_after in a batch becomes a copy published back to the stream after the delay. A small batch means small reads against the same five reads a second per shard, which poll_interval paces. A batch body reads a KinesisBatchContext, which carries the seek handle and no position of a single record. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles record by record.

Orders are stored up to 500 at a time; refunds are reviewed up to 100 at a time. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_batches.rs /// Stores a batch of orders in one round-trip and settles the whole batch with one outcome. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"))] async fn digest(batch: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = batch.len(), "orders stored"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The framework's step first, this crate's read setting after it. b.include( digest .batch(nonzero!(500)) .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(500)), ); b.include(review.batch(nonzero!(100))); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_batches.rs /// Stores a batch of orders in one round-trip and settles the whole batch with one outcome. struct Digest; impl Handle<[Order]> for Digest { fn handle( &self, batch: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = batch.len(), "orders stored"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The framework's step first, this crate's read setting after it. b.include( subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"), Digest) .batch(nonzero!(500)) .build() .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(500)), ); b.include( subscriber(KinesisStream::new("refunds"), Refunds) .batch(nonzero!(100)) .build(), ); }) }

Only the unapproved refund comes back, as a copy published after the delay. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_batches.rs /// One outcome per refund, in slice order: only the unapproved ones come back. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("refunds"))] async fn review(batch: &[Refund]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { batch .iter() .map(|refund| { if refund.approved { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect() } examples/manual/kinesis_batches.rs /// One outcome per refund, in slice order: only the unapproved ones come back. struct Refunds; impl Handle<[Refund]> for Refunds { fn handle( &self, batch: &[Refund], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { ready(Err(batch .iter() .map(|refund| { if refund.approved { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect())) } }

create_if_missing creates the stream with the shard count it names when it is missing, then waits up to a minute for it to become active. The check runs once, when the subscription opens at startup. A stream the service already has is left as it is, whatever its shard count. A missing one is created with CreateStream, and the subscription opens once the stream is active. Two instances that start together may both try to create it; the one that loses the race uses the stream the other created. A stream that is not active within the minute, or a creation the service refuses, stops the service at startup with a KinesisError::Stream that names the stream. A shard count below one is refused before any request, also at startup. Without this setting a missing stream stops the service at startup, which catches a mistyped stream name before the service runs. The setting suits local stands and tests; a production stream is usually managed as infrastructure. The service's credentials need the kinesis:CreateStream permission for it. The in-process transport of a TestApp test has every stream a service names, so there the setting changes nothing. The AsyncAPI document reports the shard count on the channel as shardCount.

On a stand without the stream parcels, the subscription creates it with two shards. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_subscriptions_create.rs /// Tracks each parcel. On a stand that lacks the stream, the subscription creates it with two /// shards before it opens. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("parcels").create_if_missing(2))] async fn track(parcel: &Parcel) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(parcel.id, "parcel tracked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("parcels", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(track); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_subscriptions_create.rs /// Tracks each parcel. On a stand that lacks the stream, the subscription creates it with two /// shards before it opens. struct Track; impl Handle<Parcel> for Track { fn handle( &self, parcel: &Parcel, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(parcel.id, "parcel tracked"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("parcels", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let parcels = KinesisStream::new("parcels").create_if_missing(2); b.include(subscriber(parcels, Track).build()); }) }

KinesisStream describes one subscription by stream name, with its read pause and the shards it provisions when the stream is missing. KinesisStream::new takes the stream name, and both settings are optional. poll_interval is the pause between reads of an idle shard, one second by default. create_if_missing creates the stream with the shards it names when the service lacks it; by default a missing stream stops the service at startup. The descriptor goes where a stream name goes: the first argument of #[subscriber], or the first argument of subscriber(source, body) in the manual form. The same two settings are also mount-site steps. The subscription's name is the stream: a test reads its deliveries under that name, and the AsyncAPI document reports that channel with both settings. A retry copy goes back to the same stream with no setting at the mount site, because a stream is both what a subscription reads and what a publish writes to.

Every payment of payments is captured; the stream is read every half second when it is quiet. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_subscriptions_stream.rs /// Captures each payment. The descriptor names the stream and the settings of its reads. #[subscriber( KinesisStream::new("payments") .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(500)) .create_if_missing(4) )] async fn capture(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment captured"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(capture); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_subscriptions_stream.rs /// Captures each payment. The descriptor names the stream and the settings of its reads. struct Capture; impl Handle<Payment> for Capture { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment captured"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let payments = KinesisStream::new("payments") .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(500)) .create_if_missing(4); b.include(subscriber(payments, Capture).build()); }) }

poll_interval sets the pause between reads of an idle shard, one second by default; the service allows five reads a second per shard. Each shard reader asks GetRecords for the next records of its shard. When a read returns records, the reader reads again at once; when a read comes back empty, it waits poll_interval first. So the setting bounds how long a new record waits on a quiet shard, and how often a quiet shard is read. The five reads a second are a limit of the shard, shared by every consumer that reads it. A read over that limit is throttled; the reader then waits one interval and reads on from where it stopped, and the handler sees a pause rather than an error. A shorter pause lowers the latency on a quiet stream and spends more of the shared limit. The same setting is a mount-site step through KinesisSubscriberExt. The AsyncAPI document reports it on the channel as pollIntervalMs.

Quotes are repriced within 200 ms of their arrival on a quiet stream. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_subscriptions_poll.rs /// Reprices on every quote. A quiet shard is read again 200 ms after an empty read, so a new /// quote waits at most that long; every read counts against the shard's five a second. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("quotes").poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(200)))] async fn reprice(quote: &Quote) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(quote.symbol, quote.price, "repriced"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("pricing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(reprice); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_subscriptions_poll.rs /// Reprices on every quote. A subscription lists its stream's shards every ten seconds, leases each one, reads it with one reader, and starts a split's children after their parents. A Kinesis stream is a set of shards, and the partition key of a record picks its shard: the service hashes the key, so one key always lands on one shard. Records of one shard are read in the order they were written, so records that share a key keep their order. Records of different shards have no order between them, and one subscription reads its shards side by side. For each shard the subscription takes a lease in the lease store; a shard another instance holds is left to that instance. The listing repeats every ten seconds, so a shard that a split or a merge adds is picked up within that time. A child shard starts only after every parent is fully read and checkpointed as finished, which keeps the order of a key across resharding. A parent the subscription never read, while it opens at the tip, does not hold its children back. How a publish names the key is on the Keys page. The in-process transport of a TestApp test keeps one shard per stream, so there every record is ordered against every other.

The stream has two shards, and each customer's shipments carry the customer as their key, so they arrive in order. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_subscriptions_shards.rs /// Ships each shipment. The stream has two shards, read side by side; a customer's shipments /// carry the customer as their partition key, so they share a shard and arrive in order. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("shipments").create_if_missing(2))] async fn ship(shipment: &Shipment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipment.customer, shipment.seq, "shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(ship); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_subscriptions_shards.rs /// Ships each shipment. The stream has two shards, read side by side; a customer's shipments /// carry the customer as their partition key, so they share a shard and arrive in order. struct Ship; impl Handle<Shipment> for Ship { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(shipment.customer, shipment.seq, "shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let shipments = KinesisStream::new("shipments").create_if_missing(2); b.include(subscriber(shipments, Ship).build()); }) }

KinesisSubscriberExt puts poll_interval and create_if_missing on the mount chain, after batch(n) and before start_at(..). The two steps are the mount-site spellings of poll_interval and create_if_missing on KinesisStream. They suit a handler whose attribute names the stream and leaves the read settings to the code that mounts it. They change the subscription's descriptor, so they need the descriptor to still be there. The framework's own steps, such as workers(n) and batch(n), come first. start_at(..) comes last: it wraps the descriptor in a start position, and the Kinesis steps are not offered after it. A handler that names its start position in the attribute names the read settings on the descriptor instead. In the manual form the steps follow .build() on subscriber(source, body).

The archive reads the whole retained stream with four workers, a 250 ms pause and a stream it creates on a bare stand. Macros Manual examples/kinesis_subscriptions_ext.rs /// Archives every audit event the stream still retains. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("audit"))] async fn archive(event: &AuditEvent) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.id, "archived"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The framework's step first, this crate's settings next, the start position last. b.include( archive .workers(nonzero!(4)) .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(250)) .create_if_missing(1) .start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()), ); }) } examples/manual/kinesis_subscriptions_ext.rs /// Archives every audit event the stream still retains. struct Archive; impl Handle<AuditEvent> for Archive { fn handle( &self, event: &AuditEvent, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.id, "archived"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The framework's step first, this crate's settings next, the start position last. b.include( subscriber(KinesisStream::new("audit"), Archive) .workers(nonzero!(4)) .build() .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(250)) .create_if_missing(1) .start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()), ); }) }

TestApp::start connects KinesisBroker in process: one retained log per stream, positions and seeking, and the service's refusals. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The in-process transport has no settings of its own. The descriptors and the publish policies of the app are the production ones, and the AWS configuration is never read. A record is written the way the publisher writes it for the service: the partition key resolved in the same order, the headers in the same envelope. It is read back by the same decoding, so a delivery carries the position, the three headers and the context a record from a shard carries. Each stream is one retained log with one shard, so every record of a stream is ordered against every other. A subscription opens at the tip, and start_at and a seek read the retained log again from the position they name. A plain retry is a requeue the stream cannot perform, so the record does not come back; a retry_after copy does, once tb.advance() passes its delay under tokio::time::pause(). The transport refuses what the service refuses. A stream name the service does not accept, a partition key outside 1 to 256 characters, and a record over 10 MiB, the most a stream can be configured to take, are refused with the service's error. A record a handler publishes there gets the error back, as it would from the service. A record the test itself publishes there fails the test at the publish. A publisher or a seek handle used after shutdown reports KinesisError::NotConnected. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, the records those handlers published included. The assertions that follow read finished state. What only the service has is for a live test: a stream's shards and the hashing of keys to them, the existence of a stream, leases and checkpoints, resharding, retention, throttling, credentials and endpoints.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-kinesis = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } The first test publishes a payment and reads how the handler settled it and what it booked on the ledger. TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against LocalStack or AWS, for shards, leases, checkpoints and resharding. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so every subscription describes its stream, lists its shards and takes its leases for real. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process transport leaves out: a stream with several shards, leases shared by two instances, checkpoints that outlive a restart, resharding and retention. A stand keeps what earlier runs left in it. The streams a service reads must exist before the app starts, unless its descriptors create them. A subscription with no checkpoint opens at the tip, so the records earlier runs left behind are not read. A test that reads the retained log, such as one on start_at, starts from a stream it recreated or from a timestamp taken when the test began. In the example, stand::endpoint returns the stand's address from KINESIS_TEST_ENDPOINT, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no stand. A job that stood a stand up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is docker-compose.test.yml, LocalStack with Kinesis and DynamoDB, which just brokers-up starts.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the stand at KINESIS_TEST_ENDPOINT.
