This guide shows what each outcome of a handler does to a shard's checkpoint, what is read again after a restart, and how a record that can never be handled is retired. Kinesis keeps no state per record and per reader. A reader remembers how far it got in each shard, its checkpoint, and starts from there next time. In RustStream the handler's outcome moves the checkpoint.

The example ships orders with a carrier. A shipment without an address can never ship. A shipment for a carrier this release of the service does not know waits for a release that knows it. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The carriers this release of the service books with. const CARRIERS: [&str; 2] = ["dhl", "ups"]; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments")] struct Shipment { id: u64, address: String, carrier: String, } #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("shipments").create_if_missing(1))] async fn ship(shipment: &Shipment) -> HandlerOutcome { if shipment.address.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(shipment.id, "shipment without an address retired"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } if !CARRIERS.contains(&shipment.carrier.as_str()) { tracing::warn!( shipment.id, shipment.carrier, "unknown carrier, shipment held" ); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(shipment.id, shipment.carrier, "shipment booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(ship); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), ) } src/main.rs /// The carriers this release of the service books with. const CARRIERS: [&str; 2] = ["dhl", "ups"]; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Shipment { id: u64, address: String, carrier: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for Shipment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "shipments"; } impl MessageHeaders for Shipment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Ship; impl Handle<Shipment> for Ship { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if shipment.address.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(shipment.id, "shipment without an address retired"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } if !CARRIERS.contains(&shipment.carrier.as_str()) { tracing::warn!( shipment.id, shipment.carrier, "unknown carrier, shipment held" ); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(shipment.id, shipment.carrier, "shipment booked"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("shipments").create_if_missing(1), Ship).build()); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(|| { service( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), ) }) }

Outcome The record The shard's checkpoint ack handled moves past it once every earlier record of the shard is handled drop retired, never read again as for ack retry, with no cap at the mount site left unhandled stops in front of it A checkpoint covers every record before it, so it advances only over a run of handled records. The crate writes it to the lease store when it moves. A record handled out of order, by a parallel lane or in a batch, moves nothing until the records before it are handled too. drop is how ship retires a shipment without an address: another try gets the same answer. retry asks Kinesis to deliver the record again, and a shard cannot do that for one record: it is a log read in order. The delivery answers AckError::Unsupported, which the runtime logs as a warning, and the record stays unhandled. ship holds a shipment for an unknown carrier this way. The reader goes on: the shipments behind it are delivered and handled, and the checkpoint waits in front of the held one. Only its own shard waits; the checkpoints of the other shards move on. Under a cap declared at the mount site, retry publishes a copy instead (Retries and dead-letter streams).

Delivery is at-least-once. A reader that takes a shard starts after its checkpoint, so everything from the first unhandled record on is delivered again: the held shipment, and every shipment behind it, handled or not. That happens when the service restarts, and when another instance takes the shard over (Several instances). So a handler that can see a record twice is written to be idempotent: booking the same shipment twice books it once. The checkpoint lives in the lease store, and the store decides what survives a restart. The default MemoryLeaseStore lives in the process and starts empty, so a restarted service opens each shard at its tip and reads only what is published from then on. DynamoLeaseStore keeps the checkpoints in a table, and a restarted service resumes where the last one stopped. A shard with no checkpoint opens at the first record its last reading read, which the store keeps beside the checkpoint. A shard nobody has read opens where start_at says, and at the tip when nothing says otherwise (Replay and seeking). A held record does not come back while the same reader holds the shard. To read it again without a restart, a handler seeks back to it.

A batch handler that returns one outcome settles every record of the batch with it. One that returns Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles each record on its own, and each moves the checkpoint of its own shard. A shard that a split or a merge closed is read to its end. Its checkpoint becomes SHARD_END only after every delivery from it is settled, and only then do its children start. A held record in a closed shard therefore holds its children back as well.

The tests in the example file run the app in process and check how each shipment settled. The in-process Kinesis keeps no checkpoints, so a held record does not come back there either. What a restart reads again runs against a stack, in the test of the Settlement example: it restarts the service over a store that outlives the first run and sees the held record first.

This guide reads a stream one record and one batch at a time, spends each shard's read budget, and shows what a delivery carries. The example is an analytics service. It books payments as they come and counts page views in batches.

A subscription runs one reader per shard it holds. The reader calls GetRecords with the shard's iterator, hands the records over in order and asks again at once. After a read that returned nothing it pauses for poll_interval, one second by default, before it asks again. At most 64 deliveries wait between the readers and the handler; a reader that finds the queue full waits, so a slow handler slows the reads down. Kinesis allows each shard five GetRecords calls a second and 2 MB a second. Every consumer of the stream shares that budget. A service that reads too often is throttled: Kinesis answers ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. The AWS SDK retries a throttled call on its own first. When the retries run out, the reader waits one poll_interval and asks again with the same iterator. The handler sees a pause, and no error and no redelivery.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments")] struct Payment { id: u64, currency: String, } /// Books the payments in euros and drops the rest, which another service books. #[subscriber( KinesisStream::new("payments") .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(250)) .create_if_missing(1) )] async fn book(payment: &Payment, Ctx(at): Ctx<Position>) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.currency != "EUR" { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(payment.id, position = ?at, "payment booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Payment { id: u64, currency: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for Payment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments"; } impl MessageHeaders for Payment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// Books the payments in euros and drops the rest, which another service books. struct Book; impl Handle<Payment, (), (), KinesisContext> for Book { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if payment.currency != "EUR" { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } let at = ctx.context(Position); tracing::info!(payment.id, position = ?at, "payment booked"); ready(Ok(())) } } book reads the payments stream and settles each payment on its own. A single subscription asks for up to 1000 records per read. poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(250)) shortens the pause after an empty read, so a new payment waits at most a quarter of a second. Four empty reads a second leave one read a second of the shard's budget to the other consumers. The setting is also a mount-site step, .poll_interval(..) after b.include(..). Ctx<Position> reads the record's place in the stream: its shard and sequence number, as a KinesisPosition. A seek to that position reads the shard again from that record (Replay and seeking). Every delivery also carries three headers: Header Value kinesis-shard-id (SHARD_HEADER) the shard the record was read from kinesis-sequence-number (SEQUENCE_HEADER) its sequence number in that shard partition-key (PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) the partition key it was published with A handler reads them with ctx.headers(). The other headers of a record are the ones its producer wrote.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "page-views")] struct PageView { page: String, } /// Counts page views a batch at a time and settles the whole batch with one outcome. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("page-views").create_if_missing(1))] async fn count(views: &[PageView]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(views = views.len(), "page views counted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct PageView { page: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for PageView { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "page-views"; } impl MessageHeaders for PageView { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// Counts page views a batch at a time and settles the whole batch with one outcome. struct Count; impl Handle<[PageView]> for Count { fn handle( &self, views: &[PageView], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(views = views.len(), "page views counted"); ready(Ok(())) } } A handler over a slice is a batch handler. The app mounts count with .batch(nonzero!(500)), and 500 becomes the limit of every GetRecords call of its readers. One read then never fetches more than one batch, and Kinesis caps a read at 10 000 records. A batch that is not full goes out 50 ms after its first record, so a quiet stream still delivers its records quickly. One batch can mix records of every shard the instance holds. The size is a trade between latency and the read budget. Small batches mean small reads, and each read spends one of the shard's five calls a second. count settles the whole batch with one outcome. A handler that returns Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles each record on its own, and each record then moves the checkpoint of its own shard (Checkpoints and delivery guarantees).

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("analytics", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(book); b.include(count.batch(nonzero!(500))); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), ) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("analytics", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber( KinesisStream::new("payments") .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(250)) .create_if_missing(1), Book, ) .build(), ); b.include( subscriber(KinesisStream::new("page-views").create_if_missing(1), Count) .batch(nonzero!(500)) .build(), ); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(|| { service( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), ) }) } A handler runs one delivery at a time by default. workers(n) in the attribute, or the workers step of the manual form, runs up to n side by side; Shards, partition keys and ordering shows how to keep the order of each key while doing so. The crate reads through the stream's shared throughput, with GetRecords. A record that the Kinesis Producer Library aggregated is not handed to a handler: the subscription reports it as KinesisError::AggregatedRecord and reads on. The tests in the example file run the app in process. The batch test starts on a paused clock, so the 50 ms a partial batch waits pass at once.
This guide installs ruststream-kinesis, starts a local Kinesis and runs a first service against it.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "json", "logging"] } ruststream-kinesis = "0.7" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-kinesis = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the default codec, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-kinesis is the Kinesis broker, built on the official aws-sdk-kinesis client. Its testing feature adds the in-process Kinesis that tests run on. The broker crate has these features, all off by default: Feature What it gives dynamodb-lease DynamoLeaseStore, so several instances of a service share the shards (Several instances) asyncapi the Kinesis details of each channel in the generated AsyncAPI document testing the in-process Kinesis behind TestApp

LocalStack runs Kinesis in one container: compose.yaml services: localstack: image: localstack/localstack:4.14.0 ports: - "4566:4566" environment: SERVICES: kinesis KINESIS_LATENCY: 0 docker compose up -d The stack answers on http://localhost:4566 and starts with no streams. KINESIS_LATENCY: 0 turns off the delay LocalStack adds to every Kinesis call by default.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders").create_if_missing(1))] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { b.include(take_order); }, ) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { b.include( subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders").create_if_missing(1), TakeOrder).build(), ); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } take_order reads JSON orders from the orders stream. It acknowledges an order with an amount and drops one without. KinesisStream names the stream, and create_if_missing(1) creates it with one shard when the subscription opens. A production service leaves that step out and takes its streams from its infrastructure. KinesisBroker::new only records the configuration. endpoint, region and test_credentials point it at the local stack. The SDK client is built when the service starts. #[ruststream::app] turns app into main; in the manual form, run_main does the same. Run the service: cargo run -- run The subscription opens at the tip of the stream, so it reads what is published after the service started. Publish an order from another terminal with the AWS CLI: export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 \ AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test aws kinesis put-record --stream-name orders --partition-key customer-7 \ --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out --data '{"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}' The service logs order taken with the order's id. Ctrl+C stops it.

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, publishes an order and checks how take_order settled it. KinesisBroker connects to an in-process Kinesis there, so the tests need no stack: cargo test Testing a Kinesis service walks through these tests and what the in-process Kinesis models.

The Rust SDK reads a stream one shard and one call at a time, and a service on it writes the consumer around those calls. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: aws-sdk-kinesis RustStream aws_config::load_from_env and Client::new KinesisBroker::new, or from_config with an SdkConfig of your own (Running in production) ListShards and a GetShardIterator per shard the stream name in KinesisStream::new; the subscription finds the shards and follows splits and merges a GetRecords loop per shard a #[subscriber] handler (Consuming a stream) decoding record.data() the handler's parameter type, decoded by the codec a checkpoint written after the work the handler's outcome (Checkpoints and delivery guarantees) a lease table so that several instances share the shards DynamoLeaseStore (Several instances) GetShardIterator with TRIM_HORIZON or AT_TIMESTAMP start_at at the mount site, or the seek handle in the handler (Replay and seeking) PutRecord with a partition key a reply or an Out parameter, sent through KinesisPublish (Shards, partition keys and ordering)

This guide runs several instances of one service on one stream, with a lease table in DynamoDB that gives each shard to one instance and keeps its checkpoint. Kinesis does not decide which consumer reads which shard. The Kinesis Client Library of other languages keeps a lease table for it, one row per shard with its owner and checkpoint. ruststream-kinesis keeps the same kind of table through a lease store.

A broker that names no store keeps its leases and checkpoints in MemoryLeaseStore, in the memory of the process. That is right for one instance. Two instances on it do not know of each other, so each reads every shard and every record is handled twice. A restarted instance starts with an empty store and opens each shard at its tip, unless start_at names another position.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream-kinesis = { version = "0.7", features = ["dynamodb-lease"] } aws-config = "1" tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] } The dynamodb-lease feature adds DynamoLeaseStore. Its table is keyed by one string attribute, lease_key, and nothing else; on-demand billing fits it. The table is infrastructure, like the stream: create it once, with Terraform, CloudFormation or the AWS CLI. On the local stack, add dynamodb to SERVICES in the compose file and create it there: aws dynamodb create-table --table-name warehouse-leases \ --attribute-definitions AttributeName=lease_key,AttributeType=S \ --key-schema AttributeName=lease_key,KeyType=HASH \ --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST One table serves every stream of a service: a row holds one shard of one stream, under the key stream:shard.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "warehouse-orders")] struct Order { id: u64, sku: String, } /// Picks each order. Every instance runs this handler, and each shard is read by the one instance /// that holds its lease. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("warehouse-orders").create_if_missing(2))] async fn pick(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.sku, "order picked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The lease store and the broker share one AWS configuration: one account, one region. fn service(config: &SdkConfig, table: &str) -> RustStream { let leases = Arc::new(DynamoLeaseStore::new(config, table)); let broker = KinesisBroker::from_config(config.clone()).lease_store(leases); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("warehouse", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(pick); }) } #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let config = aws_config::defaults(BehaviorVersion::latest()).load().await; service(&config, "warehouse-leases").run().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Order { id: u64, sku: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "warehouse-orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// Picks each order. Every instance runs this handler, and each shard is read by the one instance /// that holds its lease. struct Pick; impl Handle<Order> for Pick { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.sku, "order picked"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The lease store and the broker share one AWS configuration: one account, one region. fn service(config: &SdkConfig, table: &str) -> RustStream { let leases = Arc::new(DynamoLeaseStore::new(config, table)); let broker = KinesisBroker::from_config(config.clone()).lease_store(leases); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("warehouse", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber( KinesisStream::new("warehouse-orders").create_if_missing(2), Pick, ) .build(), ); }) } #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let config = aws_config::defaults(BehaviorVersion::latest()).load().await; service(&config, "warehouse-leases").run().await?; Ok(()) } The store and the broker take one AWS configuration, so both reach the same account and region. aws_config::defaults(..).load() reads it from the environment, and it is async, so main loads it before it builds the app and runs it with run. KinesisBroker::from_config takes the configuration, and lease_store the store. Run two copies of the service with the same environment, and they share the shards of warehouse-orders.

Each instance lists the shards when its subscription opens and again every ten seconds. It takes the lease of every shard that has no owner, or whose lease has expired, and reads those shards. A lease lasts ten seconds, and its holder renews it every three. Every write to the table is conditional, so two instances never hold one shard at once, and a checkpoint lands only while its writer holds the lease. The instances do not balance the shards between them: the one that lists first takes every free shard. The others take a shard when its holder stops, which releases its leases, or when its lease expires because the holder crashed or lost the network. An instance whose renewal fails stops reading that shard at once, without writing a checkpoint.

The instance that takes a shard over resumes after the checkpoint the last holder wrote. Records the last holder handled after its last checkpoint are delivered again, and so is a record it held and everything behind it. A shard the last holder read but never checkpointed resumes at the first record that holder read, which the table keeps in the row's opened_at column. So a takeover delivers again what the last holder read and had not settled, and skips nothing, whatever position start_at names. A restarted instance resumes the same way, since the checkpoints live in the table.

Each broker takes an owner id of its own, unique to that broker instance, and the table shows it in the lease_owner column. owner_id names the instance instead, for example after its pod. An instance that restarts under the same name gets its leases back at once, without waiting for them to expire. A fixed name must never be shared by two instances that run at the same time: both would hold the same shards and read them.

A table written by an earlier version of the crate keys its rows by the shard id alone. legacy_stream names the stream those rows belong to, so the upgraded service resumes from them. A store on another database implements LeaseStore: six calls that acquire, renew, checkpoint, record where a reading opened, read and release a lease.

The second test runs against a stack: it starts two instances on one new table, stops the first and sees the second take the shard over after the first one's checkpoint. KINESIS_TEST_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4566 cargo test -- --test-threads=1 The crate's own live tests of the lease table are in tests/leases_kinesis.rs.

This guide picks the shard of each record with its partition key, keeps the order of each key while handlers run in parallel, and keeps it when the stream reshards. The example is an order service. It posts each order to a customer's journal, four orders at a time, and confirms each journal entry with a receipt.

Every Kinesis record has a partition key. Kinesis hashes the key with MD5, and the shard whose hash key range holds the hash stores the record. Kinesis keeps the order of the records inside one shard and keeps no order between shards. So records with the same key stay in order, and records with different keys are spread over the shards. One key is one shard's throughput: a shard takes up to 1 MB or 1000 records a second. A key that carries most of the traffic makes its shard the limit of the whole stream.
documents.s: How a key picks a shard

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "customer-orders")] struct Order { id: u64, customer: String, } /// One line of a customer's journal. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "customer-orders.journal")] struct Entry { order: u64, customer: String, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Entry)] struct Journal; /// Posts each order to the journal, under the customer as its partition key. #[subscriber( KinesisStream::new("customer-orders").create_if_missing(2), workers(4, by_key) )] async fn post( order: &Order, Out(journal): Out<impl Publisher<Options = KinesisPublishOptions>, Journal>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let entry = Entry { order: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), }; if journal .message(&entry) .partition_key(order.customer.as_str()) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.customer, "order posted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Order { id: u64, customer: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "customer-orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// One line of a customer's journal. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Entry { order: u64, customer: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for Entry { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "customer-orders.journal"; } impl MessageHeaders for Entry { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Entry { const NAME: &'static str = "Entry"; } struct Journal; impl OutSlot for Journal { const NAME: &'static str = "Journal"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Journal> for Entry {} /// Posts each order to the journal, under the customer as its partition key. struct Post; impl<Lines> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Lines,)>> for Post where Lines: OutEntry<Journal, Wire: Publisher<Options = KinesisPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Lines,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let entry = Entry { order: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), }; if outs .get(Journal) .message(&entry) .partition_key(order.customer.as_str()) .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.customer, "order posted"); Ok(()) } } The shop publishes every order with the customer as its partition key, so the orders of one customer sit on one shard in the order they were placed. The customer-orders stream has two shards, and the subscription reads both side by side. workers(4, by_key) runs four lanes; deliveries with the same key run one after another on one lane. The key of a delivery is its partition key, which it carries in the partition-key header (PARTITION_KEY_HEADER). So post handles four orders at once and never two orders of one customer at the same time. In the manual form the same setting is workers_by_key. Plain workers(4) runs four deliveries at once with no regard to keys, and two orders of one customer can then finish in either order.

post writes each journal entry with partition_key(..), a step on the publish. The journal entry lands on the shard of its customer, so readers of the journal see each customer in order too. The step is a Kinesis setting, so the slot is bounded Publisher<Options = KinesisPublishOptions> to offer it. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } /// Confirms each journal entry with a receipt. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("customer-orders.journal").create_if_missing(1), reply)] async fn confirm(entry: &Entry) -> Receipt { Receipt { order: entry.order } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Receipt { order: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Receipt { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "receipts"; } impl MessageHeaders for Receipt { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Receipt { const NAME: &'static str = "Receipt"; } /// Confirms each journal entry with a receipt. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Entry, Receipt> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order: entry.order })) } } Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(post).out(Journal, Publish::default()).build(); // One key for every receipt: one shard, so the receipts keep one order between them. b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .partition_key("receipts"); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), ) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber( KinesisStream::new("customer-orders").create_if_missing(2), Post, ) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4usize)) .build(), ) .out(Journal, Publish::default()) .build(); // One key for every receipt: one shard, so the receipts keep one order between them. b.include( subscriber( KinesisStream::new("customer-orders.journal").create_if_missing(1), Confirm, ) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .partition_key("receipts"); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(|| { service( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), ) }) } A reply has no call to put a step on, so the mount site names its key on the policy: .out_reply(Publish::default()).partition_key("receipts"). Every receipt then lands on one shard, and readers see the receipts in one order, at the cost of that shard's throughput. A publish resolves its key in this order: The partition_key(..) step of the publish. The partition-key header the publish carries: written by hand, or brought along by a record from another broker of RustStream. The key the mount site named on the policy. A new key for each record, which spreads the records over the shards. The last rung keeps no order: two records published one after the other may land on different shards. The test of the example sets the key with the header, the portable spelling every broker of RustStream reads.
documents.s: Naming the key of a record

documents.t: A split closes a shard and opens two children that share its hash key range. A merge closes two adjacent shards and opens one child. The closed parents keep their records until the retention period ends. The subscription re-lists the shards every ten seconds. It starts a child only after each of its parents has been read to its end, so the records of a key stay in order across the change. A child with no checkpoint opens at its oldest record, so nothing written to it before its reader started is missed. Shards draws the parent and child shards, and the live tests of the crate split and merge a stream in tests/shards_kinesis.rs. A deferred retry publishes a copy of the record at the tip of the stream, so a retried record loses its place among the records of its key.

The tests in the example file run the app in process. The in-process Kinesis gives every stream one shard, so the test that reads the orders over two shards runs against a stack: cargo test KINESIS_TEST_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4566 cargo test -- --test-threads=1
This guide runs a Kinesis service on AWS: where its credentials and region come from, which streams it expects to find, and the IAM permissions it needs.

KinesisBroker::new() takes nothing from the code. The AWS SDK's default chain finds the region and the credentials when the service starts: environment variables, the shared ~/.aws files, SSO, and the role of the container or the instance. A service that runs under an IAM role on ECS, EKS or EC2 needs no configuration at all. The broker builds its configuration with the SDK's newest behaviour version. The SDK reads credentials when it signs its first request. That request is the check of the first subscription's stream, at startup, so a service with wrong credentials stops before it handles a record.
documents.s: Credentials and region from the environment

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The AWS configuration of the service: a pinned behaviour version, its region, and the /// credentials of the `orders-service` profile, read when the first request is signed. fn aws_config() -> SdkConfig { let credentials = ProfileFileCredentialsProvider::builder() .profile_name("orders-service") .build(); SdkConfig::builder() .behavior_version(BehaviorVersion::v2026_01_12()) .region(Region::new("eu-west-1")) .credentials_provider(SharedCredentialsProvider::new(credentials)) .build() } src/main.rs /// The AWS configuration of the service: a pinned behaviour version, its region, and the /// credentials of the `orders-service` profile, read when the first request is signed. fn aws_config() -> SdkConfig { let credentials = ProfileFileCredentialsProvider::builder() .profile_name("orders-service") .build(); SdkConfig::builder() .behavior_version(BehaviorVersion::v2026_01_12()) .region(Region::new("eu-west-1")) .credentials_provider(SharedCredentialsProvider::new(credentials)) .build() } KinesisBroker::from_config takes an SdkConfig the service builds. aws_config builds one from the environment with an async loader, while the app function is synchronous. So the example builds it with SdkConfig::builder(), which does no I/O. The profile provider reads the orders-service profile on the first request; a profile with a role_arn assumes that role. The pinned behaviour version keeps the SDK's defaults from changing under the service when the SDK is updated. The broker keeps every setting of the configuration except an endpoint or a region named on the broker itself, which replace the configuration's own. A DynamoLeaseStore takes the same configuration (Several instances). The example needs two more dependencies: Cargo.toml [dependencies] aws-config = "1" aws-sdk-kinesis = "1"

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } // The stream belongs to the infrastructure, so the descriptor does not create it. #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"))] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KinesisBroker::from_config(aws_config()), |b| { b.include(take_order); }, ) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KinesisBroker::from_config(aws_config()), |b| { // The stream belongs to the infrastructure, so the descriptor does not create it. b.include(subscriber(KinesisStream::new("orders"), TakeOrder).build()); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The orders stream belongs to the infrastructure: Terraform, CloudFormation or the console create it, with its capacity mode, retention and encryption. A stream is named by its name; the account and the region come from the configuration. The descriptor leaves out create_if_missing, so a missing stream stops the service at startup with an error that names it, instead of creating an empty one. create_if_missing(n) creates a provisioned stream with n shards, which suits a local stack; whether a production stream is provisioned or on demand is the operator's choice. Requests go over the SDK's default HTTPS client, and the SDK retries a failed request with its own retry policy. A handler on a dedicated thread (threads(n)) sends through an SDK client of its own, built from the same configuration and sharing its credentials.

The service above needs these permissions on its stream: policy.json { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "kinesis:DescribeStreamSummary", "kinesis:ListShards", "kinesis:GetShardIterator", "kinesis:GetRecords" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:kinesis:eu-west-1:123456789012:stream/orders" } ] } Each feature adds its own: Feature Permissions a publish, a reply or a retry copy kinesis:PutRecord on the stream it goes to create_if_missing kinesis:CreateStream and kinesis:DescribeStream DynamoLeaseStore dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:UpdateItem on the lease table

With the asyncapi feature, the service's AsyncAPI document names one server: the host of the broker's endpoint, or else the regional host of its region, such as kinesis.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com. A region the SDK resolves from the environment is known only at connect, after the document is built, so such a broker reports kinesis.amazonaws.com. The document never holds a credential, so it can be published. The tests in the example file start the same app in process; the in-process Kinesis signs nothing and reads no profile. Testing a Kinesis service covers the harness.

This guide reads a stream again from its oldest record or from a moment, and moves a running subscription from inside its handler. Kinesis keeps a record after a consumer has read it, until the stream's retention period ends. A service can read it again: to rebuild a read model, to backfill a new consumer, or to skip records it cannot use. A subscription takes its start position at the mount site, and a handler moves its own subscription through the delivery's context.

The service keeps two read models in memory: the balance of every account and the spend of every card. Each posting carries the ledger's revision. A correction of past postings is published as a new revision, and a read model that meets one rebuilds itself from the oldest record of the stream. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// One posting of the ledger. `revision` is the ledger's revision: a correction of past /// postings is published as a new revision, and a read model meeting one rebuilds itself. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Posting { id: u64, account: String, amount_cents: i64, revision: u32, } /// A read model kept in memory: the balance of every account. #[derive(Debug, Default)] struct Projection { revision: u32, balances: HashMap<String, i64>, } impl Projection { /// Applies `posting`, or clears the model and answers `false` when the posting belongs to a /// newer revision, which the model has to be rebuilt for from the start of the log. fn apply(&mut self, posting: &Posting) -> bool { if posting.revision > self.revision { self.revision = posting.revision; self.balances.clear(); return false; } *self.balances.entry(posting.account.clone()).or_default() += posting.amount_cents; true } } /// The service's state: one read model per subscription that builds one. #[derive(Clone, Default)] struct Projections { balances: Arc<Mutex<Projection>>, spend: Arc<Mutex<Projection>>, } src/main.rs /// One posting of the ledger. `revision` is the ledger's revision: a correction of past /// postings is published as a new revision, and a read model meeting one rebuilds itself. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Posting { id: u64, account: String, amount_cents: i64, revision: u32, } /// A read model kept in memory: the balance of every account. #[derive(Debug, Default)] struct Projection { revision: u32, balances: HashMap<String, i64>, } impl Projection { /// Applies `posting`, or clears the model and answers `false` when the posting belongs to a /// newer revision, which the model has to be rebuilt for from the start of the log. fn apply(&mut self, posting: &Posting) -> bool { if posting.revision > self.revision { self.revision = posting.revision; self.balances.clear(); return false; } *self.balances.entry(posting.account.clone()).or_default() += posting.amount_cents; true } } /// The service's state: one read model per subscription that builds one. #[derive(Clone, Default)] struct Projections { balances: Arc<Mutex<Projection>>, spend: Arc<Mutex<Projection>>, }

The balances live in memory, so after a restart they are built again from the whole stream. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber( KinesisStream::new("ledger").create_if_missing(1), start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()) )] async fn project_balance( posting: &Posting, ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisContext, Projections>, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let applied = ctx .state() .balances .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .apply(posting); if applied { tracing::info!(posting.id, "balance updated"); return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } tracing::info!( posting.id, posting.revision, "new revision, rebuilding the balances" ); if seeker.seek(KinesisPosition::horizon()).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Declaring `KinesisContext` is what puts the seek handle in the context. struct ProjectBalance; impl Handle<Posting, (), (), KinesisContext, Projections> for ProjectBalance { async fn handle( &self, posting: &Posting, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisContext, Projections>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let applied = ctx .state() .balances .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .apply(posting); if applied { tracing::info!(posting.id, "balance updated"); return Ok(()); } tracing::info!( posting.id, posting.revision, "new revision, rebuilding the balances" ); if ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(KinesisPosition::horizon()) .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()) opens every shard at its trim horizon, the oldest record the stream still keeps. It applies on every start, to the shards the subscription opens with, ahead of any stored checkpoint. Without start_at, a shard resumes after its checkpoint and opens at its tip when it has none. KinesisPosition has four positions: Position Where the subscription reads from horizon() the oldest record of every shard latest() the tip of every shard, so only new records are read timestamp(ms) the first record of every shard that arrived at or after ms sequence(shard, seq) one record of one shard, and the records after it A stream keeps its records for 24 hours by default, and up to 365 days with extended retention. What is past the retention period is gone, and the trim horizon moves forward with it.

The same handler rebuilds the balances when a posting of a newer revision arrives. Ctx<SeekHandle> gives the handler the KinesisSeeker of its own subscription. seek moves the subscription to the oldest record, and the handler reads every posting again. The posting that started the rebuild comes back as well, and this time the projection applies it. A seek takes any of the positions above. A position for the whole stream moves every shard this instance holds. Ctx<Position> holds the delivery's own position, a sequence position: a seek there reads that shard again from the record and moves no other shard. It needs this instance to hold the shard; a seek to a shard that another instance reads, or that is finished, fails.

Card postings arrive in volume, so the spend is built in batches of up to 500. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("card-postings").create_if_missing(1))] async fn project_spend( postings: &[Posting], ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisBatchContext, Projections>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let applied = { let mut spend = ctx .state() .spend .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner); postings.iter().all(|posting| spend.apply(posting)) }; if applied { tracing::info!(postings = postings.len(), "card spend updated"); return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } tracing::info!("new revision, rebuilding the card spend"); if ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(KinesisPosition::horizon()) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// A batch body declares `KinesisBatchContext`, which carries the same seek handle. struct ProjectSpend; impl Handle<[Posting], (), (), KinesisBatchContext, Projections> for ProjectSpend { async fn handle( &self, postings: &[Posting], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KinesisBatchContext, Projections>, ) -> Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>> { let applied = { let mut spend = ctx .state() .spend .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner); postings.iter().all(|posting| spend.apply(posting)) }; if applied { tracing::info!(postings = postings.len(), "card spend updated"); return Ok(()); } tracing::info!("new revision, rebuilding the card spend"); if ctx .context(SeekHandle) .seek(KinesisPosition::horizon()) .await .is_err() { return Err(postings.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()).collect()); } Ok(()) } } A batch handler declares KinesisBatchContext instead of the per-delivery context. It carries the same SeekHandle key and no position, because a batch spans many records. A body that needs the place of one record reads its kinesis-shard-id and kinesis-sequence-number headers.

The payout review reads the payouts of the last day on every start. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// A payout as the payments service publishes it. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Payout { id: u64, amount_cents: i64, } #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("payouts").create_if_missing(1))] async fn review_payout(payout: &Payout) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(payout.id, payout.amount_cents, "payout reviewed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// A payout as the payments service publishes it. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Payout { id: u64, amount_cents: i64, } /// The body reads no context, but runs in an app whose state is `Projections`. struct ReviewPayout; impl Handle<Payout, (), (), (), Projections> for ReviewPayout { fn handle( &self, payout: &Payout, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Projections>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(payout.id, payout.amount_cents, "payout reviewed"); ready(Ok(())) } } The moment is known only when the service starts, so the mount site names the position instead of the attribute. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Milliseconds since the epoch, the unit of a Kinesis arrival timestamp. fn epoch_millis(at: SystemTime) -> u64 { at.duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map_or(0, |since| { u64::try_from(since.as_millis()).unwrap_or(u64::MAX) }) } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker, review_from: SystemTime) -> impl App<State = Projections> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Projections::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(project_balance); b.include(project_spend.batch(nonzero!(500usize))); b.include( review_payout.start_at(KinesisPosition::timestamp(epoch_millis(review_from))), ); }) } /// The review reads the payouts of the last day on every start, the stream's default retention. const REVIEW_WINDOW: Duration = Duration::from_hours(24); #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Projections> { let review_from = SystemTime::now() - REVIEW_WINDOW; service( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), review_from, ) } src/main.rs /// Milliseconds since the epoch, the unit of a Kinesis arrival timestamp. fn epoch_millis(at: SystemTime) -> u64 { at.duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map_or(0, |since| { u64::try_from(since.as_millis()).unwrap_or(u64::MAX) }) } fn service(broker: KinesisBroker, review_from: SystemTime) -> impl App<State = Projections> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Projections::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber( KinesisStream::new("ledger").create_if_missing(1), ProjectBalance, ) .start_at(KinesisPosition::horizon()) .build(), ); b.include( subscriber( KinesisStream::new("card-postings").create_if_missing(1), ProjectSpend, ) .batch(nonzero!(500usize)) .build(), ); b.include( subscriber( KinesisStream::new("payouts").create_if_missing(1), ReviewPayout, ) .start_at(KinesisPosition::timestamp(epoch_millis(review_from))) .build(), ); }) } /// The review reads the payouts of the last day on every start, the stream's default retention. const REVIEW_WINDOW: Duration = Duration::from_hours(24); fn app() -> impl App<State = Projections> { let review_from = SystemTime::now() - REVIEW_WINDOW; service( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), review_from, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } KinesisPosition::timestamp takes milliseconds since the epoch. Kinesis matches it against the arrival timestamp it stamped on each record. That stamp is approximate, so records that arrived around the same moment are not told apart exactly.

A seek clears the checkpoint bookkeeping of every shard it moves. A delivery read before the seek settles into nothing, so the ack of the posting that started the rebuild moves no checkpoint. A later checkpoint therefore never passes a record that the seek replayed and no handler has handled yet. A seek moves this instance only: other instances keep reading the shards they hold, and an instance that takes a shard over resumes from its checkpoint. The tests in the example file run the app in process. The in-process Kinesis keeps the whole log of each stream, so a seek reads it again there too.

This guide retries a record now or later, caps the attempts and moves what keeps failing to a dead-letter stream. Kinesis does not hold a record back, does not count deliveries and has no dead-letter queue. The framework does all three: the mount site declares the cap and the dead-letter stream, and a retry travels as a copy of the record with a retry count in a header. The example is a refunds service that sends refunds through a card processor.

The processor refuses a refund in three ways, and each needs a different outcome. Busy means its rate limit is used up: a retry right now would be refused again, so retry_after waits 30 seconds. Unavailable means it did not answer: retry tries again at once. Declined means the card account is closed, and another try gets the same answer, so the refund is dropped. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "refunds")] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("refunds").create_if_missing(1))] async fn process_refund( refund: &Refund, State(processor): State<Arc<Processor>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { match processor.refund(refund).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Refund { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "refunds"; } impl MessageHeaders for Refund { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct ProcessRefund; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for ProcessRefund { async fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match ctx.state().processor.refund(refund).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } } retry_after settles the record and publishes a copy back to refunds once the delay has passed. The copy carries the retry-count header (RETRY_COUNT_HEADER), raised by one. The copy waits in the service's memory, so it is at-most-once: a process that stops before the delay ends loses it, and the original is already behind the checkpoint. retry under a declared cap also becomes a copy, published at once. Without a cap it holds the shard's checkpoint in front of the record, as Checkpoints and delivery guarantees shows.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // Five deliveries of one refund, the first included; then the dead-letter stream. b.include(process_refund) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.review"); b.include(review); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { service( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), ) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: KinesisBroker) -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // Five deliveries of one refund, the first included; then the dead-letter stream. b.include( subscriber( KinesisStream::new("refunds").create_if_missing(1), ProcessRefund, ) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.review"); b.include( subscriber( KinesisStream::new("refunds.review").create_if_missing(1), Review, ) .build(), ); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(|| { service( KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), ) }) } max_attempts counts every delivery of one refund, the first included. The fifth delivery is not retried: dead_letter publishes it to refunds.review, payload and headers as they arrived. A cap without a dead-letter stream checkpoints past the spent record instead, as drop does. A dropped refund settles and goes nowhere; the dead-letter stream holds only the refunds that ran out of attempts. The streams belong to the service's infrastructure; the example creates them with create_if_missing for a local stack.

documents.t: The dead-letter stream is an ordinary stream, and review reads it like any other. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(KinesisStream::new("refunds.review").create_if_missing(1))] async fn review(refund: &Refund, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(refund.id, deliveries, "refund needs a person to look at it"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Review; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for Review { fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(refund.id, deliveries, "refund needs a person to look at it"); ready(Ok(())) } } The retry-count header of a dead-lettered record holds the number of deliveries it went through, 5 here. review reads it with ctx.headers() and logs the refund for a person to look at.

A copy goes back to the stream the subscription reads, so a registration on Kinesis needs no retry destination of its own. It keeps the record's partition key, so it lands on the shard of that key. It lands at the tip of that shard, though, after the records published while it waited. A refund that waits 30 seconds is therefore handled after the refunds of the same card that came later. Where the order of a key matters more than moving on, declare no cap and let retry hold the shard: the checkpoint stops at the record, and the shard is read again from it when its lease is next taken. out_retry replaces the publisher the copies leave through, so a transform can stamp each copy on its way out.

The tests in the example file run the app in process with a paused clock, so tb.advance(BACKOFF) lets the 30 seconds pass at once. TestApp::with_state starts the app with a stand-in processor that is busy or silent. Testing a Kinesis service covers the harness.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, against an in-process Kinesis or against a stack. The service under test charges card payments. A payment arrives on card-payments, and its partition key is the account to charge. The handler replies with a receipt on card-receipts. A payment without an amount is dropped. A payment over the bank's instant limit is held: the handler asks for it again in a minute with retry_after. After three deliveries a payment goes to card-payments.review, the dead-letter stream. The app is built by service(broker), so a test chooses the broker and main uses the production one. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-kinesis in [dev-dependencies].

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_keyed_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(KinesisBroker::new())).await?; a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb).await } async fn a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .with_headers(keyed("acct-7")) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: 1, account: "acct-7".to_owned(), }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_keyed_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(KinesisBroker::new())).await?; a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb).await } async fn a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .with_headers(keyed("acct-7")) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: 1, account: "acct-7".to_owned(), }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } TestApp::start connects KinesisBroker to an in-process Kinesis. No AWS endpoint is called, and no credentials are needed. The test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>(). The partition key of a record travels as the partition-key header (PARTITION_KEY_HEADER), so the test sets it with with_headers. The broker turns that header into the record's partition key, and the delivery reports it back under the same header. publish returns once the handler and its reply have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscriber settled and what reached card-receipts. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the live test below runs it too.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_without_an_amount_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(KinesisBroker::new())).await?; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 2, amount_cents: 0, }) .with_headers(keyed("acct-7")) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_without_an_amount_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(KinesisBroker::new())).await?; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 2, amount_cents: 0, }) .with_headers(keyed("acct-7")) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } settled checks the outcome the handler returned. assert_not_called checks that no receipt was published.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_payment_the_bank_keeps_holding_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(KinesisBroker::new())).await?; let held = Payment { id: 3, amount_cents: 250_000, }; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .message(&held) .with_headers(keyed("acct-7")) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The delay is a copy of the record, published back to the stream after `HOLD`. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments") .assert_called(2) .with(&held) .with_header(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, "1") .with_header(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, "acct-7"); // The third delivery is the last one: it goes to the review stream as it arrived. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack], ); tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments.review") .assert_called_once() .with(&held); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_payment_the_bank_keeps_holding_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(KinesisBroker::new())).await?; let held = Payment { id: 3, amount_cents: 250_000, }; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .message(&held) .with_headers(keyed("acct-7")) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The delay is a copy of the record, published back to the stream after `HOLD`. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments") .assert_called(2) .with(&held) .with_header(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, "1") .with_header(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, "acct-7"); // The third delivery is the last one: it goes to the review stream as it arrived. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack], ); tb.broker::<KinesisBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments.review") .assert_called_once() .with(&held); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } The test starts on a paused clock, and advance moves it forward. A minute of HOLD costs nothing. Kinesis cannot hold a record back, so retry_after publishes a copy of the record to its stream when the delay ends. The copy carries the retry count and the record's partition key in its headers, and published shows it on card-payments next to the test's own record. The third delivery is the last one the mount site allows, so the record goes to card-payments.review as it arrived. Each held delivery is recorded as Outcome::Nack.

documents.t: The in-process Kinesis writes and reads records the way the service does for the broker. The same partition-key rules apply, user headers ride the same envelope, and a delivery carries the same headers and context as one from a shard: A broker reads a stream through one subscription, which reads every record of it and opens at the tip; a second subscription to the stream is refused, as the service's broker refuses it. start_at and the handler's seek handle read the stream's log again from the position they name (Replay and seeking). retry with no cap is answered as Kinesis answers it, unsupported, and the record does not come back. A deferred retry comes back as a counted copy, and a spent record goes to the dead-letter stream. A record the service refuses is refused: a stream name over 128 characters or outside [a-zA-Z0-9_.-], a partition key that is empty or over 256 characters, a record over 10 MiB, the most a stream can be configured to take. A test that publishes one fails with the service's error. A publisher or a seek handle used after shutdown reports KinesisError::NotConnected. Every stream has one shard there, so every record is ordered against every other, and every stream a service names exists. Several shards, leases and checkpoints, retention and resharding need a stack.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_keyed_payment_gets_a_receipt_on_a_stack() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(endpoint) = support::endpoint() else { return Ok(()); }; // The service reads `card-payments` and creates it; the receipts are only published. support::ensure_stream(&support::config(&endpoint).await, "card-receipts", 1).await; let broker = KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint(endpoint) .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(); let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(broker)).await?; a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb).await } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_keyed_payment_gets_a_receipt_on_a_stack() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(endpoint) = support::endpoint() else { return Ok(()); }; // The service reads `card-payments` and creates it; the receipts are only published. support::ensure_stream(&support::config(&endpoint).await, "card-receipts", 1).await; let broker = KinesisBroker::new() .endpoint(endpoint) .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(); let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(broker)).await?; a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb).await } TestApp::start_live connects the same app to a running Kinesis, here LocalStack. A publish waits up to ten seconds for the reaction to settle; start_live_within sets a longer deadline. The test reads the endpoint from KINESIS_TEST_ENDPOINT with support::endpoint, a helper of the examples, and skips when it is unset. The service creates card-payments when its subscription opens; the test creates card-receipts, which only receives. The subscription opens at the tip, so records an earlier run left in the stream are not read. The assertions are the in-process ones, unchanged. cargo test KINESIS_TEST_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4566 cargo test -- --test-threads=1
